claims.claim: Electrically-evoked EPSPs had higher paired-pulse ratios than ChR2-evoked EPSPs and were mildly facilitating at short (20 ms) intervals.
claims.source: Electrically-evoked EPSPs had higher paired-pulse ratios than ChR2-evoked EPSPs and were mildly facilitating at short (20 ms) intervals (Figure 3B–C, open circles: n=5 cells, 3 mice), consistent with an octopus cell's ability to respond reliably to click trains in vivo (Godfrey et al., 1975; Rhode et al., 1983; Smith et al., 2005; Oertel et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 3B-C and compared to previous in vivo studies.

claims.claim: ChR2-evoked synaptic responses undergo synaptic depression.
claims.source: ChR2-evoked synaptic responses are known to undergo synaptic depression (Jackman et al., 2014; Zhang and Oertner, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Electrically evoked EPSPs with non-physiological calcium concentrations (2.4 mM) resulted in short-term depression at 50 Hz of electrical stimulation.
claims.source: We repeated paired-pulse plasticity experiments with non-physiological calcium concentrations (2.4 mM) and similarly found that electrically evoked EPSPs from SGNs resulted in short-term depression at 50 Hz of electrical stimulation (Figure 3C, grey: n=3 cells, 2 mice), although not to the degree observed when using full-field, ChR2-evoked inputs (Figure 3C, black: n=8 cells, 5 mice).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Light-evoked (Slc6a5-ChR2) inhibitory post synaptic potentials (IPSPs) were not observed in octopus cell somas during whole-cell current clamp recordings from P30-45 mice under control conditions.
claims.source: Similarly, we did not observe light-evoked (Slc6a5-ChR2) inhibitory post synaptic potentials (IPSPs) in octopus cell somas during whole-cell current clamp recordings from P30-45 mice.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claims.claim: Pharmacologically reducing conductances from voltage-gated potassium (Kv) and hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels increased octopus cell membrane resistance and hyperpolarized the resting membrane potential by ~8–10 mV.
claims.source: This cocktail increased octopus cell membrane resistance and hyperpolarized the resting membrane potential by ~8–10 mV (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The increase in input resistance unveiled light-evoked IPSPs in recordings from octopus cell somas.
claims.source: Consistent with our hypothesis, the increase in input resistance unveiled light-evoked IPSPs in recordings from octopus cell somas (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Light-evoked IPSPs were fully abolished by bath application of 500 nM strychnine (STN), confirming the presence of functional glycinergic inhibitory synaptic transmission onto octopus cells.
claims.source: Additionally, these IPSPs were fully abolished by bath application of 500 nM strychnine (STN) (Figure 4C), confirming the presence of functional glycinergic inhibitory synaptic transmission onto octopus cells.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Relevant glycine receptors include both large conductance extrasynaptic β-subunit lacking homomeric receptors and synaptically localized α2β receptors with slower kinetics.
claims.source: These results indicate that relevant glycine receptors include both large conductance extrasynaptic β-subunit lacking homomeric receptors and synaptically localized α2β receptors with slower kinetics (Lynch, 2009; Veruki et al., 2007; Dutertre et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from pharmacological experiments and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Removal of Kv and HCN conductances in the model changed the input resistance and current-voltage relationship of the neuron, resulting in reduced electrotonic isolation.
claims.source: As in our current-clamp recordings (Figure 4A), removal of Kv and HCN conductances in the model changed the input resistance and current-voltage relationship of the neuron, resulting in reduced electrotonic isolation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Activation of large (10nS) dendritic glycinergic conductances induced negligible hyperpolarizing voltage changes in the model.
claims.source: Activation of large (10nS) dendritic glycinergic conductances induced negligible hyperpolarizing voltage changes in the model (Figure 4F, black).
claims.evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: With increased input resistance and reduced electrotonic isolation after Kv and HCN block, dendritic IPSPs measured at the soma were detectable.
claims.source: With increased input resistance and reduced electrotonic isolation after Kv and HCN block, dendritic IPSPs measured at the soma were detectable (Figure 4F, blue), consistent with our in vitro recordings.
claims.evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 4F that matches experimental data.

claims.claim: Kv and HCN block increased the magnitude of soma-measured IPSPs for all glycine conductances.
claims.source: Kv and HCN block and the resulting change in input resistance increased the magnitude of soma-measured IPSPs for all glycine conductances (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: Following the pharmacological blockade of Kv and HCN channels, there was either a reduction in the amplitude of inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) at distal synapses or little change in IPSC amplitude at proximal synapses.
claims.source: In contrast, following the pharmacological blockade of Kv and HCN channels, we observed either a reduction in the amplitude of inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) at distal synapses (Figure 4H, blue) or little change in IPSC amplitude at proximal synapses (Figure 4H, orange).
claims.evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: Alterations in IPSCs are unlikely to account for the observed increase in inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP) magnitude recorded at the soma after Kv and HCN channel block.
claims.source: These findings indicate that alterations in IPSCs are unlikely to account for the observed increase in inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP) magnitude recorded at the soma after Kv and HCN channel block (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I–J).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the modeling results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1I–J.

claims.claim: Transfer impedance (ZT), a measure of signal transmission efficiency, was dramatically increased after Kv and HCN block.
claims.source: Transfer impedance (ZT), a measure of signal transmission efficiency, was dramatically increased after Kv and HCN block (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K).
claims.evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1K.

claims.claim: Inhibitory synapses that are located proximally to excitation had less of an influence on excitation recorded at the soma compared to those inhibitory synapses located distally to excitation.
claims.source: In our model, inhibitory synapses that are located proximally to excitation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) had less of an influence on excitation recorded at the soma compared to those inhibitory synapses located distally to excitation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The model predicted that inhibition reduces EPSP amplitude and accelerates EPSP peak timing at the soma for both inhibition proximal to excitation and inhibition distal to excitation.
claims.source: For both inhibition proximal to excitation (Figure 5B–C) and inhibition distal to excitation (Figure 5D–E), the model predicted that inhibition reduces EPSP amplitude and accelerates EPSP peak timing at the soma.
claims.evidence: This is a result from computational modeling shown in Figure 5B-E.

claims.claim: When synaptic inhibition was evoked together with excitation, EPSPs recorded in the soma were smaller and faster than when excitation was evoked alone.
claims.source: When synaptic inhibition was evoked together with excitation (Figure 5F, green), EPSPs recorded in the soma were smaller and faster than when excitation was evoked alone (Figure 5F, black: n=8 cells, 6 mice).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: ChR2-evoked inhibition decreased EPSP heights by 25.2 ± 9.0% and shifted the peak of EPSPs forward 57.5 ± 26 µs.
claims.source: ChR2-evoked inhibition decreased EPSP heights by 25.2 ± 9.0% (Figure 5G, green) and shifted the peak of EPSPs forward 57.5 ± 26 µs (Figure 5H, green).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative experimental result shown in Figure 5G-H.

claims.claim: Bath application of 25 µM glycine mimicked the effect of ChR2-evoked inhibition on EPSPs.
claims.source: This effect was mimicked by bath application of 25 µM glycine (Figure 5G–H, blue: n=4 cells, 3 mice).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 5G-H.

claims.claim: Bath application of 1 µM STN resulted in larger EPSPs and delayed peak times.
claims.source: Further, bath application of 1 µM STN had the opposite effect, resulting in larger EPSPs and delayed peak times (Figure 5F–H, orange: n=5 cells, 4 mice).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 5F-H.

claims.claim: The timing of EPSP arrival in the soma may be shaped both by tonically active glycine channels and the release of synaptic glycine onto the dendrite.
claims.source: These findings suggest that the timing of EPSP arrival in the soma may be shaped both by tonically active glycine channels and the release of synaptic glycine onto the dendrite.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results with glycine and strychnine.

claims.claim: Many SGNs terminate on the octopus cell soma, where inhibition is minimal.
claims.source: Of note, many SGNs also terminate on the octopus cell soma, where inhibition is minimal.
claims.evidence: This is based on the anatomical data showing high excitatory and low inhibitory puncta density on the soma.

claims.claim: The octopus cell's ability to act as a coincidence detector depends on two stages of compartmentalized computations, one in the dendrite that combines excitation and inhibition and one in the soma that is restricted by the rigid temporal summation window for coincidence detection.
claims.source: This suggests that the octopus cell's ability to act as a coincidence detector depends on two stages of compartmentalized computations, one in the dendrite that combines excitation and inhibition to provide important information about which frequencies co-occur in a complex sound stimulus and one in the soma that is restricted by the rigid temporal summation window for coincidence detection.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, integrating all the experimental and modeling results.

claims.claim: Octopus cells respond well to cues that include complex spectrotemporal patterns, including frequency modulations beyond the onset of the stimulus.
claims.source: As shown by in vivo recordings (Recio-Spinoso and Rhode, 2020; Lu et al., 2022), octopus cells respond well to cues that include complex spectrotemporal patterns, including frequency modulations beyond the onset of the stimulus (Lu et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous in vivo recording studies.

claims.claim: The addition of dendritic inhibition transforms the magnitude and timing of SGN signals as they arrive in the cell body, which may expand the response selectivity of an octopus cell.
claims.source: The results suggest that, in addition to high Kv and HCN conductances at rest, the addition of dendritic inhibition transforms the magnitude and timing of SGN signals as they arrive in the cell body, which may expand the response selectivity of an octopus cell and allow them to become a slightly leakier integrator that can accumulate evidence beyond onsets.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental and modeling results.

claims.claim: The majority of inputs onto octopus cells come from Ia SGNs, which most closely correspond to the low-threshold, high-spontaneous rate population.
claims.source: We find that the majority of inputs onto octopus cells come from Ia SGNs, which most closely correspond to the low-threshold, high-spontaneous rate population.
claims.evidence: This is based on the quantitative anatomical data showing Ia SGN dominance.

claims.claim: Single-unit SGN recordings in cats demonstrated a bias towards low-threshold, high-spontaneous rate axon collaterals in the octopus cell area.
claims.source: Consistent with this result, single-unit SGN recordings in cats demonstrated a bias towards low-threshold, high-spontaneous rate axon collaterals in the octopus cell area (Liberman, 1993).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work in cats.

claims.claim: Low-threshold SGNs are characterized by short first spike latencies and low temporal jitter.
claims.source: Low-threshold SGNs are also characterized by short first spike latencies and low temporal jitter (Buran et al., 2010; Oliver et al., 2006; Bourien et al., 2014; Costalupes et al., 1984).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The presence of many low-threshold and temporally precise inputs on the octopus cell may help ensure that coincidence detection still works reliably for quiet sounds.
claims.source: The presence of many low-threshold and temporally precise inputs on the octopus cell may help ensure that coincidence detection still works reliably for quiet sounds.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of Ia SGNs and their dominance on octopus cells.

claims.claim: Ia inputs onto octopus cells do not exhibit paired-pulse depression, similar to low levels of depression seen in Ia inputs to bushy cells.
claims.source: Further, Ia inputs onto octopus cells do not exhibit paired-pulse depression, similar to low levels of depression seen in Ia inputs to bushy cells (Zhang et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is based on the experimental data and supported by a citation to work on bushy cells.

claims.claim: Recruitment of higher threshold SGNs at higher sound intensities may compensate for saturation of precise, low-threshold SGN responses by background noise.
claims.source: Since precise, low-threshold SGN responses can be saturated by background noise such that responses to relevant stimuli are masked (Liberman, 1978; Costalupes et al., 1984; Bourien et al., 2014; Huet et al., 2016), recruitment of higher threshold SGNs at higher sound intensities may compensate for this tradeoff.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of different SGN subtypes and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Resting conductances and low-threshold potassium conductances may suppress voltage-gated calcium spikes and attenuate the magnitude of action potentials as they backpropagate through the soma and dendritic tree in octopus cells.
claims.source: Resting conductances and low-threshold potassium conductances may suppress voltage-gated calcium spikes and attenuate the magnitude of action potentials as they backpropagate through the soma and dendritic tree (Golding et al., 1999; Cao and Oertel, 2005; Bal and Baydas, 2009; Bal and Oertel, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Subthreshold dendritic integration of coincident excitation and local inhibition may be the primary computation that occurs in octopus cell dendrites before action potential generation near the soma.
claims.source: Therefore, subthreshold dendritic integration of coincident excitation and local inhibition may be the primary computation that occurs in octopus cell dendrites before action potential generation near the soma.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the biophysical properties of octopus cells.

claims.claim: It is unknown where glycinergic innervation to octopus cells originates.
claims.source: Although this work uncovers a role for inhibition, a deeper understanding of octopus cell computations will require determining what information is carried by inhibitory inputs. Despite the well-established presence of presynaptic glycinergic puncta in the octopus cell area (Kemmer and Vater, 1997; Kolston et al., 1992; Juiz et al., 1996; Moore et al., 1996) and glycinergic receptor expression in octopus cells (Friauf et al., 1997; Sato et al., 2000; Schofield and Cant, 1996; Thompson et al., 1985; Adams and Mugnaini, 1987), it is unknown where glycinergic innervation originates.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge despite previous anatomical studies.

claims.claim: It remains unclear whether octopus cells receive connections from D-Stellate, L-Stellate, or tuberculoventral cells.
claims.source: Local neurons within the CNC could provide inhibition; however it remains unclear whether octopus cells receive connections from D-Stellate (Oertel et al., 1990), L-Stellate (Ngodup et al., 2020), or tuberculoventral cells (Wickesberg et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: This is stated as uncertain and supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Terminal degeneration experiments in cats suggested the superior periolivary nucleus (SPON) and the ventral division of the lateral lemniscus (VNLL) as potential sources of descending inhibition to the octopus cell area.
claims.source: Outside of the CNC, terminal degeneration experiments in cats suggested the superior periolivary nucleus (SPON) and the ventral division of the lateral lemniscus (VNLL) as potential sources of descending inhibition to the octopus cell area (Kane, 1977).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work in cats.

claims.claim: Octopus cells provide excitatory input to both the SPON and the VNLL.
claims.source: Octopus cells provide excitatory input to both the SPON (Friauf and Ostwald, 1988; Schofield, 1995; Thompson and Thompson, 1991; Zook and Casseday, 1985; Felix Ii et al., 2017) and the VNLL (Schofield and Cant, 1997; Smith et al., 2005; Berger et al., 2014; Nayagam et al., 2005; Adams, 1997; Vater and Feng, 1990), raising the possibility of feedback inhibition from the auditory brainstem as a circuit mechanism that elongates temporal summation windows during ongoing stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Descending feedback inhibition is not rapid enough to prevent or alter the characteristic octopus cell onset response, but could change the effective coincidence detection window as the stimulus continues or limit the duration of the response.
claims.source: Such descending feedback inhibition is not rapid enough to prevent or alter the characteristic octopus cell onset response, but could change the effective coincidence detection window as the stimulus continues or limit the duration of the response.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the potential role of feedback inhibition.

results.result: Octopus cells receive a higher density of excitatory SGN inputs (10.7 ± 3.0 puncta/100 µm²) than inhibitory inputs (4.2 ± 0.8 puncta/100 µm²) on dendrites, with a strikingly different ratio of excitatory to inhibitory puncta on the soma (7:1) versus dendrites (5:2). The average octopus cell receives ~1035 SGN synapses and ~354 inhibitory synapses, with 83% of synapses on dendrites.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C13, C18-C19, and C43 provide converging quantitative anatomical evidence from 3D reconstructions showing differential distribution of excitatory and inhibitory synapses across somatic and dendritic compartments. The measurements are internally consistent and include appropriate sample sizes (n=8-9 cells from multiple mice) with reported variability.

results.result: The majority of SGN inputs onto octopus cells come from type Ia SGNs (62 ± 9.7% of synapses), which correspond to low-threshold, high-spontaneous rate neurons. Ib/c SGNs account for 38% of inputs despite comprising 60.1% of the total SGN population, indicating Ia SGNs are overrepresented on octopus cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C17, C47-C48 provide consistent evidence from genetic labeling, cell counting (n=1599 neurons), and synaptic reconstruction showing Ia SGN dominance. The findings align with previous cat studies (C48), strengthening the conclusion. The quantitative measurements are well-documented with appropriate controls.

results.result: SGN inputs to octopus cells exhibit mild facilitation at high frequencies (50 Hz) when assessed with electrical stimulation under physiological conditions, but show paired-pulse depression with ChR2 stimulation or non-physiological calcium concentrations. Ia inputs do not exhibit paired-pulse depression.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C23 and C51 provide experimental evidence distinguishing physiological from artifactual synaptic properties. The comparison between electrical and optogenetic stimulation methods (C20-C21) and calcium concentration effects (C23) appropriately controls for technical confounds. Statistical testing shows no differences between total and Ib/c populations (p>0.35), supporting the conclusion about Ia inputs.

results.result: Functional glycinergic inhibitory synaptic transmission onto octopus cells was revealed by pharmacologically blocking Kv and HCN channels to increase input resistance. Light-evoked IPSPs were fully abolished by strychnine, confirming glycinergic transmission involving both homomeric and α2β heteromeric receptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C28 provide a logical experimental progression: initial failure to detect IPSPs (C24), pharmacological manipulation to increase detection (C25-C26), confirmation with antagonists (C27), and receptor subtype characterization (C28). The approach is well-controlled with appropriate pharmacology (n=6-9 cells from multiple mice).

results.result: Computational modeling demonstrates that dendritic IPSPs are electrically isolated from the soma under control conditions due to low input resistance, but become detectable after Kv and HCN block due to increased transfer impedance rather than changes in local IPSC amplitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C35 provide comprehensive computational evidence supporting the experimental findings. The model appropriately accounts for passive and active properties, demonstrates that increased transfer impedance (C35) rather than IPSC changes (C33-C34) explains somatic IPSP detection, and matches experimental observations (C31). The modeling approach is rigorous and well-validated.

results.result: Dendritic inhibition reduces EPSP amplitude by 25.2 ± 9.0% and advances EPSP peak timing by 57.5 ± 26 µs at the soma. Both computational modeling and experiments with coincident excitation and inhibition demonstrate that inhibition shapes EPSP timing, with effects mimicked by bath glycine application and reversed by strychnine.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C42 provide converging evidence from modeling (C36-C37) and experiments (C38-C41) showing consistent effects of inhibition on EPSP properties. The quantitative measurements (C39) are supported by pharmacological controls (C40-C41, n=4-8 cells). The inference about tonic and synaptic glycine (C42) is reasonable given the strychnine effects.

results.result: Octopus cells employ a two-stage compartmentalized computation: dendritic integration of excitation and inhibition that modulates EPSP timing and amplitude, followed by somatic coincidence detection within a narrow temporal window. This mechanism allows responses to both rapid onsets and frequency modulations during ongoing sounds.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C3, C44, and C46 represent the main conclusions integrating all experimental and modeling results. The two-stage computation model is well-supported by the anatomical distribution of synapses, the functional demonstration of dendritic inhibition effects, and the preservation of somatic coincidence detection properties. This is the central finding of the manuscript.

results.result: Low-threshold Ia SGNs are characterized by short first spike latencies and low temporal jitter, properties that may ensure reliable coincidence detection for quiet sounds. Recruitment of higher threshold SGNs at higher intensities may compensate for saturation of low-threshold responses by background noise.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C50 and C52 are supported by citations to previous physiological studies (C49) and represent reasonable inferences based on the demonstrated Ia SGN dominance and known properties of SGN subtypes. The logic connecting low-threshold properties to reliable detection (C50) and intensity compensation (C52) is sound, though these remain functional predictions.

results.result: Octopus cells respond to complex spectrotemporal patterns including frequency modulations beyond stimulus onset. Subthreshold dendritic integration of coincident excitation and inhibition may be the primary computation in dendrites, as resting conductances likely suppress dendritic spikes and backpropagation.
results.evaluation: Claim C45 is supported by citations to in vivo studies. Claims C53-C54 represent reasonable inferences based on known biophysical properties (supported by citations in C53) and the experimental findings of this study. The conclusion about subthreshold integration (C54) is consistent with the lack of evidence for dendritic spiking in octopus cells.

results.result: The source of glycinergic inhibition to octopus cells remains unknown, though potential sources include local CNC neurons (D-Stellate, L-Stellate, tuberculoventral cells) or descending feedback from SPON and VNLL. Feedback inhibition could modulate coincidence detection windows during ongoing stimuli without affecting onset responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C59 acknowledge gaps in knowledge and propose potential sources based on anatomical studies (C57-C58). However, these remain speculative (C56, C59) as the current study does not identify inhibitory sources. The proposals are reasonable but require future experimental validation through circuit tracing or manipulation studies.

results.result: Octopus cells are specialized coincidence detectors with low input resistance (~4 MΩ), fast time constants (~200 µs), and narrow coincidence detection windows (~1 ms) that allow them to detect momentary coincidence of excitatory inputs and phase lock to broadband transients up to 1 kHz. SGNs project tonotopically to the cochlear nucleus and include physiologically distinct subtypes recruited at different intensities.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C4-C10 establish the background knowledge about octopus cells and the auditory system, all supported by appropriate citations to previous work. These claims provide essential context for the current study's findings and are well-established in the literature.

results.result: The authors used immunohistochemistry and genetic labeling to quantify excitatory (SGN) and inhibitory (glycinergic) synaptic inputs across the soma and dendrites of individual octopus cells. They found that octopus cells receive both excitatory and inhibitory inputs, with different ratios on soma (7:1) versus dendrites (5:2), and that 83% of synapses are located on dendrites.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly praises this work, stating 'the analysis of synaptic distribution and the origin of the excitatory inputs stands as one of the most complete descriptions of any neuron, leaving little doubt about the presence of glycinergic boutons.' All reviewers accept these anatomical findings without critique.

results.result: The authors characterized three molecularly distinct SGN subtypes (Ia, Ib, Ic) and quantified their relative contributions to octopus cell innervation, finding that Ia SGNs (low-threshold, high-spontaneous rate) account for 62% of SGN synapses on octopus cells despite comprising only ~40% of the total SGN population.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 commends the 'beautiful immunohistochemical and mouse genetic methods to quantify the inhibitory and excitatory boutons' and notes the analysis of 'the proportions of the different subtypes of spiral ganglion cell inputs.' No reviewer questions these findings.

results.result: The authors examined short-term synaptic plasticity of SGN inputs using optogenetic and electrical stimulation, finding no paired-pulse depression in ChR2-evoked responses from total or Ib/c SGN populations, while electrically-evoked EPSPs showed mild facilitation at short intervals.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these electrophysiological findings. Reviewer 3 notes the study 'clarify the presence of functional inhibition and elucidate some of the features of the inhibitory inputs to octopus cells at a biophysical level' without raising concerns about the synaptic plasticity data.

results.result: The authors demonstrated that inhibitory inputs to octopus cells were initially undetectable under control conditions but became visible after pharmacologically blocking Kv and HCN channels to increase input resistance. The revealed IPSPs were abolished by strychnine, confirming glycinergic transmission.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 acknowledges 'the authors have tried to overcome these limitations using drugs to block leak conductances' to address the 'enormous leak currents that shunt membrane stimuli.' Reviewer 3 states the study provides 'convincing evidence that octopus cells do in fact receive glycinergic synaptic input.'

results.result: Using computational modeling, the authors showed that Kv and HCN conductances create strong electrotonic isolation that normally masks dendritic IPSPs at the soma. Blocking these conductances increased transfer impedance and made dendritic IPSPs detectable, consistent with experimental observations.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes 'The modeling is better described, which is critical because it provides a foundation to help interpret some of the physiology.' Reviewer 1 mentions the authors used 'computational approaches based on realistic parameters' without raising concerns about the modeling results.

results.result: Through combined modeling and experiments, the authors demonstrated that dendritic inhibition reduces EPSP amplitude by ~25% and advances EPSP peak timing by ~58 microseconds. These effects were confirmed with optogenetic inhibition, bath glycine application, and strychnine blockade.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 states the study shows 'through modeling that inhibition is predicted to both provide shunting of synaptic currents and to change the peak timing of dendritic EPSPs as they travel to the soma. Both of these effects are potentially critically important in integration in these fast, coincidence-detecting neurons, and the magnitudes of the effects could have physiological significance.'

results.result: The authors conclude that dendritic inhibition enhances coincidence detection by enabling two-stage compartmentalized computation: dendritic integration of excitation and inhibition provides information about frequency co-occurrence, while somatic integration maintains strict temporal summation for coincidence detection. This allows octopus cells to respond to both rapid onsets and frequency modulations during ongoing sounds.
results.evaluation: The editor states the study 'convincingly demonstrate that octopus cells...receive glycinergic inhibitory synaptic inputs that influence their synaptic integration' and that 'inhibition can shunt synaptic currents and alter the timing of dendritic EPSPs, both of which are significant for auditory processing.' Reviewer 3 notes the work 'extends thinking about the functional sensory processing roles of octopus cells beyond the pre-existing hypotheses.'

results.result: The authors discuss the functional implications of Ia SGN dominance on octopus cells, proposing that low-threshold, temporally precise Ia inputs ensure reliable coincidence detection for quiet sounds, while recruitment of higher-threshold Ib/c SGNs at higher intensities compensates for saturation of Ia responses by background noise.
results.evaluation: These interpretations are presented as discussion points supported by citations and the authors' data. No reviewer challenges these functional interpretations, and Reviewer 1 specifically praises the completeness of the synaptic characterization that underlies these conclusions.

results.result: The authors acknowledge that the source of glycinergic inhibition to octopus cells remains unknown, discussing potential local sources (D-Stellate, L-Stellate, tuberculoventral cells) and descending sources (SPON, VNLL) as possibilities for future investigation.
results.evaluation: These are explicitly presented as open questions and speculation by the authors. Reviewers do not critique this as a limitation, implicitly accepting that identifying the source of inhibition is beyond the scope of the current study.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on the main conclusions (C2, C3, C44, C46). Both evaluations find the two-stage computation model well-supported. OpenEval emphasizes integration of experimental and modeling results, while peer reviewers highlight the extension of functional understanding beyond pre-existing hypotheses. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Divergent evaluations of the same claims (C55-C59) about inhibitory sources. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting these are speculative and require future validation. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting that identifying inhibitory sources is beyond scope and appropriately presented as open questions. Different interpretation of how to evaluate acknowledged speculation.

Strong agreement on computational modeling (C29-C32, C34-C35). Both find the modeling rigorous and well-validated. OpenEval emphasizes that transfer impedance rather than IPSC changes explains somatic IPSP detection. Peer reviewers praise improved model description and realistic parameters. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Strong agreement on inhibition effects on EPSP properties (C36-C41). Both find converging evidence from modeling and experiments. OpenEval notes quantitative measurements with pharmacological controls. Peer reviewers emphasize physiological significance of shunting and timing effects for coincidence detection. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Strong agreement on anatomical findings (C11-C13, C18-C19). OpenEval emphasizes quantitative consistency and appropriate sample sizes. Peer reviewers describe this as 'one of the most complete descriptions of any neuron.' OpenEval also includes C43 not mentioned in peer review. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Strong agreement on Ia SGN dominance (C14-C17, C47). OpenEval emphasizes genetic labeling, cell counting, and alignment with cat studies. Peer reviewers praise the immunohistochemical and genetic methods. OpenEval also includes C48 not in peer review. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Strong agreement on pharmacological detection of IPSPs (C24-C27). OpenEval emphasizes the logical experimental progression and controls. Peer reviewers acknowledge the approach to overcome leak current limitations and find convincing evidence of glycinergic input. OpenEval also includes C28 on receptor subtypes. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Agreement on electrophysiological methods (C20-C21, C23). OpenEval emphasizes control for technical confounds and statistical testing. Peer reviewers accept findings without challenge, noting clarification of functional inhibition. OpenEval also includes C22 and C51 not mentioned in peer review. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Agreement on functional interpretations (C49-C50, C52). OpenEval notes these are reasonable inferences based on Ia SGN dominance and known SGN properties, though remaining functional predictions.
